claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The initial Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
The dynamic mechanical behavior of Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed by a temperature- and strain-rate-dependent transition between stacking-fault-assisted twinning and dislocation cross-slip.
Low temperature and high strain rate reduce thermal activation and suppress dislocation cross-slip.
Suppression of cross-slip favors accumulation of partial dislocations and stacking faults.
Accumulated stacking faults promote deformation twinning.
Twin structures impede dislocation motion and thereby increase strength and strain hardening.
Twin-boundary networks can also provide pathways for dislocation motion, permitting substantial plastic deformation and contributing to high ductility.
Increasing temperature thermally activates additional dislocation cross-slip.
Enhanced cross-slip at elevated temperature reduces twin density.
Enhanced cross-slip produces more homogeneous dislocation flow and preserves a favorable strength-ductility balance.
Relative to quasi-static room-temperature loading, high-strain-rate loading at low temperature will produce higher twin and stacking-fault densities.
The higher twin and stacking-fault densities predicted at low temperature and high strain rate will correlate with increased strain hardening and strength.
Elevated-temperature loading will produce stronger signatures of cross-slip and lower twin density than the room-temperature baseline.
Elevated-temperature loading will moderately reduce strain hardening while maintaining ductility.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to conditions where Co-free FeNiCrMn remains a single-phase solid solution and excludes phase transitions and recrystallization.

In situ high-speed X-ray or neutron diffraction, supplemented by direct imaging or slip-band analysis, can be used to compare twin density, stacking-fault density, cross-slip indicators, and stress-strain behavior across temperature and strain-rate conditions.

Failure to observe increased stacking-fault and twin densities under low-temperature, high-strain-rate loading, or observation of cross-slip dominance at all temperatures, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
